summary: Casinos and gaming are splitting into three stories. Macao is growing only slowly: October gross gaming revenue fell 10% and is down five months in a row, though year to date it is up 1.6% [9]. Las Vegas is soft, with Strip win up under 1% in September [18]. Online betting is growing fast but is being squeezed by taxes and a new rival, prediction markets: DraftKings cut 2026 guidance and Flutter cut its guide and paused buybacks [2][4]. Equipment makers look steadier, with Aristocrat at 39% share of North American machines and Light & Wonder margins at 46% [7][8]. DraftKings is down about 33% this year [17].

DraftKings and Flutter are both funding prediction-market products, with DraftKings guiding a $650M to $700M 2026 EBITDA investment and Flutter about $200M [2][4].
Flutter's leverage is 4.6x, its buyback is paused and the UK remote gaming duty rose from 21% to 40% [4].
Caesars is being acquired by Fertitta Entertainment, a deal announced on 28 May 2026 that will take the company private [5].

basics.intro: This sub-industry covers companies that take bets or sell the means to bet. Casino operators own resorts and earn money when customers lose a small, statistically predictable share of what they wager, plus hotel, food and entertainment sales. Online betting companies do the same on phones. Equipment makers sell or lease slot machines and table games to casinos and run social and online games. GICS puts hotel brands and cruise lines in the next sub-industry, and real estate owners such as casino landlords sit in real estate.

products.name: Integrated resorts and casinos
products.what: Large properties combine a casino floor with hotels, convention space, shopping and shows. Gambling is the profit engine and the other parts fill the building and attract customers.
products.examples: Las Vegas Sands (Macao, Singapore), Wynn, MGM Resorts, Caesars

products.name: Regional casinos
products.what: Casinos close to home markets that draw repeat local customers, often with a loyalty card. They have steadier visits than destination resorts.
products.examples: Caesars regional casinos, MGM regional properties

products.name: Online sports betting
products.what: Apps take bets on sports and keep the difference between what is wagered and what is paid out, after promotions. It is legal state by state in the US.

products.name: Online casino (iGaming)
products.what: Slots and table games played on a phone. Margins are higher than sports betting but it is legal in only a few US states.
products.examples: DraftKings Casino, FanDuel Casino, BetMGM, Light & Wonder iGaming

products.name: Slot machines and gaming systems
products.what: Makers build the cabinets and games, then sell them or lease them to casinos for a share of daily win. They also sell the software that runs the floor.

products.name: Social casino games
products.what: Free-to-play casino-style mobile games that earn money from in-app purchases rather than wagers.

terms.meaning: What players wagered minus what they won back, before costs and often before promotions. Regulators publish it monthly for places such as Macao and Nevada.
The share of money wagered that the casino keeps. It is fixed by game design over the long run but swings in any one quarter, which is why results are often shown as hold-adjusted.
Total amount bet with a sportsbook. Revenue equals handle times the net revenue margin.
Sportsbook revenue as a share of handle after payouts and promotions. It moves with how often favourites win, so one bad weekend can change a quarter.
High-stakes players, especially baccarat players in Macao and Singapore. They bring large volumes but also large swings in results.
Operating profit before depreciation and other items. EBITDAR also adds back rent, which matters for operators that lease their casinos from real estate landlords.
Free bets and bonuses given to win or keep online customers. Heavy promotion cuts reported revenue and profit, especially when a company launches in a new state or product.
The number of distinct customers who bet in a month. DraftKings reports it as its core customer count.
The number of machines a maker has on casino floors. Leased machines earn a recurring share of the daily win, so a rising base means steadier revenue.
An exchange where people trade contracts on whether events happen, including sports results. Betting companies see it as a rival way to wager that is regulated federally rather than state by state.
The share of gaming revenue paid to governments. Rates are set by each jurisdiction and are one of the biggest swing items for online betting profits.
The government permission to run casinos in a place such as Macao or Singapore. Licences are limited and renewed on set dates, which gives incumbents protection and the government leverage.

drivers.name: Visitor numbers and spending
drivers.how: Destination casinos depend on trips to Macao, Singapore and Las Vegas. When travel or consumer budgets weaken, occupancy, room rates and gaming volumes all fall together.

drivers.name: Luck (hold) in the short run
drivers.how: A few large bets can move a quarter's profit. Companies and analysts therefore adjust for hold, and results can miss or beat without any change in demand.

drivers.name: Taxes and regulation
drivers.how: A rate rise cuts the profit on every dollar of online revenue. Legalisation in a new state or country opens a market, while a ban closes it overnight.

drivers.name: Customer acquisition cost
drivers.how: Online companies spend heavily on advertising and promotions to win customers. Profit rises when spending falls relative to revenue, as mature customers keep betting.

drivers.name: Leverage and interest rates
drivers.how: Casino building is expensive and mostly debt-funded. Higher rates raise interest costs, which eat into the profit that EBITDA does not show.

drivers.name: Casino capital spending cycle
drivers.how: Equipment makers sell more when casinos refit floors or open new resorts and less when owners conserve cash, so machine sales can swing even when play is steady.

business: Casino operators earn gaming revenue from slots and tables plus rooms, food, retail and entertainment. Online operators earn sportsbook and iGaming revenue; DraftKings' third-quarter revenue was $783.6M from sports and $460.9M from iGaming [2]. Equipment makers earn from machine sales, leased machines and games on mobile, as at Light & Wonder, where gaming operations were $248M and machine sales $199M in the quarter [7].

Customers are tourists and high-stakes players at destination resorts, local repeat players at regional casinos, and app users online. DraftKings had 4.1M monthly unique payers [2], and Flutter's US business had 3.9M average monthly players [4]. Equipment makers sell to casino operators, so their customers are the operators themselves.

Costs are labour, gaming taxes, marketing and, for physical resorts, property upkeep and interest. For online firms, marketing and promotions are the largest swing. Flutter attributed weaker International profit mainly to the UK remote gaming duty rising from 21% to 40% [4], which shows how much tax matters.

Pricing power comes from licences, location and brand. A resort in a limited-licence market like Singapore or Macao has protected demand: Marina Bay Sands earned a 45.6% EBITDA margin in the quarter [1]. Online, pricing power is weaker because odds are shopped and bonuses are matched, so scale and product depth decide who earns a margin.

Main assets are casino buildings, land, gaming licences, machines and customer databases. Main liabilities are debt: Las Vegas Sands had $15.30B in debt [1], Wynn $10.73B [6], Caesars $11.66B [5] and Flutter $12.3B in total debt [4]. Customer deposits and player funds also sit on the balance sheets of online firms.

Resort operators are capital-intensive, with Las Vegas Sands spending $281M in a single quarter on its Macao and Singapore properties [1]. Online betting is asset-light but spends heavily on marketing instead. Equipment makers sit between the two, since leased machines tie up capital while sold machines and software need little.
overview: No single global size figure was available from a source I opened. In the US, AGA counts commercial gaming revenue of $78.72B in 2025, up 9.2%, a fifth straight record [10]. Macao, the largest single gaming centre, reported MOP208.8B of gross gaming revenue for January to October 2026, up 1.6% [9].

Main segments are land-based casinos, sports betting, iGaming, and equipment and games. AGA's 2025 split: sports betting $16.96B up 23%, iGaming $10.74B up almost 28%, and legacy casinos, racinos and riverboats $50.95B up 2% [10]. Online is the fast-growing piece; land-based is the base.

The value chain runs from equipment makers and software suppliers to casino and online operators, then to players. Aristocrat and Light & Wonder sell to operators, who sell to consumers [7][8]. Governments sit in the chain as licensor and tax collector, taking for example 40% on UK remote gaming from Flutter's International business [4].

The industry started with land-based casinos in Nevada and Macao, expanded through Asian integrated resorts, then added online. The US market opened in 2018 when states could legalise sports betting, and by DraftKings' count mobile sports betting is live in 27 states plus D.C. and Puerto Rico, covering about 53% of the US population [2]. Prediction markets are the newest entrant [4].

Sales are concentrated in the US, Macao, Singapore and Europe. Las Vegas Sands' Macao net revenue was $1,940M and Marina Bay Sands $1,294M in the quarter [1], while MGM China contributed $1.14B [3]. Flutter's International business, led by the UK, brought in $2.42B [4]. iGaming is legal in only five states, about 11% of the US population [2].
competition: There are a few dozen significant listed competitors, with the largest being Las Vegas Sands, Flutter, Aristocrat, MGM, Caesars, Wynn, DraftKings and Light & Wonder, all of which reported results this season [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8]. Many smaller regional and tribal operators and private companies also compete, though no source I opened counts them.

Leaders by segment: in Macao there are six licensed casino operators sharing the market [9]; Aristocrat puts its share of North American machines at 39% [8]; FanDuel and DraftKings lead US online betting, but I did not find a sourced market-share split for them. Flutter's US revenue was $1.455B in the quarter against DraftKings' $1.329B total [2][4].

Online betting and equipment are consolidated at the top, while land-based casinos are mixed. Caesars' pending takeover by Fertitta Entertainment, announced 28 May 2026, is one more sign of consolidation among operators [5]. Land-based casinos are local monopolies or oligopolies in many places.

Barriers to entry are high where licences are limited, as in Macao's six-operator market [9], and where building a resort costs billions. Online barriers are lower on technology but high on brand, licences by state and marketing spend, which is why Flutter and DraftKings are pouring money into promotions [2][4].

Economies of scale are large. Bigger online firms spread technology, risk-management and marketing over more users; bigger resort companies spread loyalty programmes over more properties. Aristocrat's installed base grew about 6,500 machines in North America in FY26 [8], which helps it supply more titles and place more machines.

Products are partly commoditised. A bet on a football game is the same anywhere, so online competition runs through promotions, odds and product features. Slot machines and casino resorts are more differentiated through game content, brand and location. Aristocrat and Light & Wonder compete on game performance, with Light & Wonder's Gaming segment margin at 56% [7].

Customers have little bargaining power individually but can switch apps freely, which forces promotion spending. Governments have strong power as licensors and taxers. Casino operators have power over equipment makers when they hold off on capital spending, and Light & Wonder's gaming systems revenue fell 24% [7]. Equipment suppliers have concentration on their side.
drivers: Revenue growth comes from visitor volume, spend per visit, new legal markets and new capacity. DraftKings' consumer volume rose 21.9% [2], and Flutter's US handle rose 13% [4]. New buildings such as Wynn Al Marjan Island in the UAE, expected in September 2027, add capacity [6].

Operating margins depend on hold, the mix of premium players, promotions and taxes. Las Vegas Sands' consolidated margin fell to 34.8% from 40.3%, partly from lower Marina Bay Sands volume [1], while Wynn's Las Vegas table win of 18.9% fell below its expected 22% to 26% range [6].

Key costs are labour, gaming taxes, marketing, interest and, for equipment makers, product development. DraftKings' non-GAAP tax rate is 27%, up from 23% in 2025 [2]. For online players, marketing and promotion is the biggest controllable cost, with Predictions alone expected to cost $650M to $700M in 2026 at DraftKings [2].

Interest rates matter because operators are heavily indebted. Caesars paid $570M of net interest in the quarter against $2.94B of revenue [5], and Flutter's leverage is 4.6x [4]. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October, with two members preferring a hike [16], so refinancing is not getting cheaper.

Inflation hurts through costs and consumer spending. The Fed says inflation remains elevated, while job gains have kept pace with the workforce [16]. Gaming responds to consumer discretionary budgets: MGM's Las Vegas Strip EBITDAR fell 12% [3], and Strip gaming win rose only 0.82% in September [18]. Commodities matter little.

Gaming is cyclical at the destination end, since it relies on travel and discretionary income, but it holds up better than many leisure categories at regional level. Online betting and iGaming are secular growth, with AGA showing sports betting up 23% and iGaming up almost 28% in 2025 [10], though growth is now clouded by tax rises and prediction markets.
financials: Growth varies a lot by segment. DraftKings' third-quarter revenue rose 16.2% [2], Flutter's 2% [4], Light & Wonder's fell 2% [7], MGM's fell 1% [3] and Wynn's fell 7.9% on the figures published [6]. Earnings are volatile: Flutter and DraftKings each reported net losses, at $1,148M and $468.7M [4][2].

Damodaran's January 2026 data for 63 US Hotel/Gaming firms (which includes hotels, not only casinos) shows a 60.85% gross margin, 24.45% EBITDA margin and 10.38% net margin [12]. Among the largest companies, Las Vegas Sands earned 34.8% and Light & Wonder 46% on adjusted EBITDA [1][7].

Damodaran lists an unadjusted ROE of 45.38% for Hotel/Gaming [13]. That is inflated by high debt and buybacks, so it needs caution; the table I opened did not show ROIC for this group. Interest coverage is only 3.06 by Damodaran's measure, which says returns on capital are thinner than ROE suggests [14].

Debt is high. Damodaran shows gross debt to EBITDA of 5.30 and book debt to capital of 82.27% for the group [14]. Company levels: Flutter 4.6x [4], Light & Wonder 3.3x net with a target below 3.0x [7], Caesars net debt of $10.80B [5]. Las Vegas Sands had $2.86B of cash against $15.30B of debt [1].

Free cash flow is solid at mature operators. Light & Wonder produced adjusted free cash flow of $181M in the quarter and $545M year to date [7], and Las Vegas Sands repurchased $950M of stock in the quarter [1]. Online firms are less settled: DraftKings had cash of $1,100.9M and total adjusted EBITDA of negative $316.9M in the quarter [2].

Capital expenditure is heavy for resort developers: Wynn expects $750M to $800M of Macau project capex plus $475M to $525M of UAE equity contributions in 2027 [6]. Las Vegas Sands spent $281M in the quarter [1]. Online betting firms need less physical capital but spend on technology and marketing.

Damodaran's January 2026 data shows EV/EBITDA of 14.93x for US Hotel/Gaming firms with positive EBITDA and 17.70x for all firms [11]. These are group multiples, not casino-only ones, and are a start date reference rather than current prices. DraftKings was about 22x forward earnings in early November [17].
risks: Regulation is the largest single risk. The UK remote gaming duty rose from 21% to 40% [4], Brazil banned online sports betting and iGaming and Flutter closed its operations there on 26 September [4], and DraftKings' tax rate rose [2]. Macao's concessions also depend on government terms, which we did not research further.

Technology and AI matter less than regulation, but online products are software, and prediction markets show how a new technology wrapper can shift where bets are placed. DraftKings counted over 1.6M customers engaged with Predictions in 2026 [2], and FanDuel Predicts had 66k average monthly players in Q3 [4]. We found no sourced AI-specific disruption estimate.

Demographics help online betting, since younger customers are comfortable on apps, and Light & Wonder's SciPlay says 31% of its revenue now comes direct-to-consumer [7]. For land-based casinos, the customer base is tied to travel flows. We found no sourced demographic projection for the industry.

Consumer behaviour is shifting. Las Vegas visitation was flat in September and Strip win rose only 0.82% [18], MGM's Strip EBITDAR fell 12% [3], and Macao's October revenue fell 10% despite the Golden Week holiday [9]. Customers are choosing between destinations and between apps on price and promotion.

New competitors include prediction-market exchanges and new online brands. Flutter's CEO says the impact on existing customers is limited, but rivals are raising its media costs [17], and both Flutter and DraftKings are spending to build their own products [2][4]. If prediction markets keep growing, we think they could limit pricing power for sportsbooks.

Geopolitical risk shows up in Macao, which depends on mainland Chinese visitors, and in Wynn's UAE project, which is a Middle East bet [6][9]. Supply chains matter little for operators, and I found no sourced supply-chain issue for equipment makers [7].

Substitutes include other leisure spending, illegal offshore betting and prediction markets. Macao's decline despite the Golden Week holiday suggests spending is not following visits [9]. Social casino is a partial substitute too, with SciPlay revenue down 12% [7], so not all digital play is a gain for casinos.

opportunities: More US states may legalise online betting and iGaming, since only five have iGaming today, covering about 11% of the population [2].
Operating leverage in online betting: DraftKings guides adjusted EBITDA to $800M to $1.0B in 2027 from $175M to $275M in 2026 [2].
New resorts and capacity, including Wynn Al Marjan Island in the UAE (expected September 2027) [6].
Equipment makers can grow installed bases, as Aristocrat did by about 6,500 North American machines in FY26 [8].
threats: Higher taxes and bans, as shown by the UK duty rise to 40% and the Brazil closure [4].
Prediction markets taking customers or raising costs, with DraftKings and Flutter both spending heavily to compete [2][4][17].
Weak Macao demand, with five straight monthly declines and CICC seeing no clear near-term inflection point [9].
High debt in a higher-for-longer rate environment, with Flutter at 4.6x and Caesars at $10.80B of net debt [4][5][16].
horizon.assessment: Over the next three to five years we think the sector's growth is likely to come from online betting, new legal markets and a handful of new resorts, while the main uncertainties are tax, prediction markets and the pace of Macao's recovery. DraftKings guides to a swing from $175M to $275M of EBITDA in 2026 to $800M to $1.0B in 2027 [2], but that depends on Predictions spending coming down. Resort operators are mature, with strong cash returns at Las Vegas Sands [1] and heavy debt elsewhere [4][5]. Equipment makers look steadiest to us [7][8].

paragraphs: The macro backdrop is cautious rather than weak. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October 2026, with two members voting for a quarter-point increase, and its statement says inflation remains elevated while job gains have kept pace with the workforce [16]. For an industry that owns expensive buildings and carries heavy debt, that is not an easing cycle.

The cycle is hitting destinations unevenly. Las Vegas Strip gaming win rose only 0.82% in September to $693.5M [18], and MGM's Strip EBITDAR fell 12% [3]. Caesars' Las Vegas revenue fell 2.3% while its regional segment grew 5.9% [5].

Macao is the clearest weak spot. Gross gaming revenue was MOP21.68B in October, down 10% year on year and the fifth straight monthly decline, even with the National Day Golden Week holiday, though January to October is still up 1.6% [9]. We read that as spending per visitor and premium play lagging visit counts. Currency matters for firms reporting in dollars against Macao patacas and sterling, but we found no sourced estimate.

Structural demand is strongest online. AGA counted US commercial gaming revenue of $78.72B in 2025, up 9.2%, with sports betting up 23% to $16.96B and iGaming up almost 28% to $10.74B, while legacy casinos, racinos and riverboats grew 2% to $50.95B [10]. Land-based play is a mature base and the growth is in apps.

Footprint explains the headroom. DraftKings says mobile sports betting is live in 27 states plus D.C. and Puerto Rico, about 53% of the US population, and iGaming in five states, about 11% [2]. Legalisation of iGaming is the main way to add revenue, though we found no sourced forecast for which states will move.

Demand is partly elastic. Customers can cut trips or stakes when budgets tighten, and Macao's October decline despite the Golden Week holiday suggests spend per head matters more than headcount [9]. DraftKings' sports consumer volume grew 21.9% in the third quarter and its monthly unique payers rose about 13% to 4.1M [2], while Flutter's average monthly players fell 3% group-wide, with a 12-point hit from exiting India [4].

For the long term we think demand for betting is durable but not guaranteed to stay with today's licensed operators. Prediction markets, where over 1.6M DraftKings customers have already engaged with its own Predictions product, show the product can move to a different regulatory wrapper [2].

Using Porter's five forces: the threat of new entrants is low in licence-limited resorts, such as Macao's six operators [9], and moderate online, where brands and state licences matter. Customers hold bargaining power online because they can compare odds and switch apps, which forces promotions; Flutter says rival prediction markets are already raising its media costs [17].

Supplier power sits with governments and, to a degree, equipment makers. Aristocrat holds about 39% of the North American market and grew its installed base by around 6,500 units in FY26 [8], while Light & Wonder's Gaming segment earns a 56% margin [7]. Casino operators can respond by delaying purchases, and Light & Wonder's guidance toward the low end of its range points to softer capital demand [7].

Substitutes are rising: prediction markets, other leisure, illegal betting and social casino, where SciPlay revenue fell 12% [7]. Rivalry among existing firms is intense online, where DraftKings is guiding to a $650M to $700M Predictions investment in 2026 [2] and Flutter to about $200M [4].

Concentration is rising. Caesars is due to be taken private by Fertitta Entertainment under a deal announced on 28 May 2026 [5]. The moats are licences, locations, loyalty databases and game content; in our view the strongest are Singapore and Macao licences, evidenced by Marina Bay Sands' 45.6% EBITDA margin [1], and Aristocrat's installed-base position [8].

Regulation is the dominant factor. Flutter closed Brazil on 26 September 2026 after a Provisional Measure banned online sports betting and iGaming, taking an $873M non-cash impairment, and the UK remote gaming duty went from 21% to 40% [4]. DraftKings' non-GAAP tax rate is 27% against 23% in 2025 [2]. We found no sourced figure for how many US states raised taxes this year.

Politically, prediction markets are the open fight. They are a federally regulated alternative to state-licensed betting. Flutter plans to launch FanDuel Predicts in December in states without regulated sports betting [4], and DraftKings expects Predictions revenue of $650M to $750M in 2027 with an EBITDA investment of $250M to $350M [2]. I did not open a primary source on court rulings, so I will not characterise the legal state of play.

Technological change comes through mobile products, direct-to-consumer apps and online play. Light & Wonder's iGaming revenue grew 13% and SciPlay's direct-to-consumer share reached 31% of its revenue [7]. Aristocrat Interactive revenue rose 3.4% [8].
Geopolitically, Macao depends on mainland visitors and Wynn is building in the UAE, with 40% ownership and $1.12B contributed so far [6][9].

Economics differ by business model. Equipment makers earn high margins: Light & Wonder's consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin was 46% and the Gaming segment's 56% [7]. Resort operators earn mid-range margins: Las Vegas Sands' consolidated margin was 34.8% (Macao 27.3%, Marina Bay Sands 45.6%) [1]. Damodaran's group average for Hotel/Gaming is 24.45% EBITDA margin [12].

Operating leverage is high. A small drop in volume or hold removes large profit, as at Las Vegas Sands where revenue fell 3% but adjusted property EBITDA fell 17% to $1,119M [1], or at Wynn where revenue fell 7.9% and adjusted property EBITDAR fell 18.6% [6]. Online firms show it in reverse as revenue grows faster than fixed costs, but promotions can swamp that.

Capital intensity is highest for resorts. Las Vegas Sands spent $281M in the quarter [1] and Wynn guides $750M to $800M of Macau capex for 2027 [6]. Returns are hard to read: Damodaran lists a 45.38% unadjusted ROE for Hotel/Gaming [13], but with 82.27% book debt to capital and 3.06x interest coverage [14], we think that flatters the picture. I did not find a sourced ROIC for the sub-industry.

Free cash flow is strong at the equipment makers: Light & Wonder produced $545M year to date [7]. Resort groups use cash for buybacks and development, as Las Vegas Sands' $950M repurchase and $5.06B remaining authorisation show [1]. Online players are still investing: DraftKings' third-quarter adjusted EBITDA was negative $316.9M [2].

Earnings are being cut at the online companies and are mixed at resorts. DraftKings lowered 2026 revenue guidance to $6.35B to $6.55B and adjusted EBITDA to $175M to $275M, and Flutter lowered group adjusted EBITDA guidance to a $2.495B midpoint, down $160M, citing unfavourable sports results and the Brazil closure [2][4]. Las Vegas Sands' diluted EPS was $0.48 against $0.61 a year earlier, and adjusted EPS $0.54 against $0.78 [1].

Management guidance for next year is where the debate sits. DraftKings guides 2027 revenue of $7.35B to $7.75B and adjusted EBITDA of $800M to $1.0B, with a core-business EBITDA of $1.15B to $1.25B before the Predictions investment [2]. Flutter says it will spend as much or more on its prediction market in 2027 [17]. Light & Wonder expects 2026 adjusted EBITDA growth toward the low end of its mid-to-high single-digit range [7].

Aristocrat expects constant-currency NPATA growth again in FY27 after 9.7% growth in FY26 [8]. MGM's Strip EBITDAR fell 12% but BetMGM's share of operating income rose to $26.7M from $23.7M [3]. Caesars Digital EBITDA rose 57% to $44M while Las Vegas EBITDA fell 9.5% [5].

I did not find consensus EPS growth for this sub-industry in a source I opened, so I cannot say where our view differs. Our read is that the 2027 recovery implied by DraftKings' guide depends on spending discipline, and the guidance cuts show how fragile estimates have been this year [2][4].

We found no sourced forward P/E for this sub-industry alone. As a market reference, FactSet puts the S&P 500 at 17.7x forward 12-month earnings on 5 November 2026, against a 5-year average of 19.8x and a 10-year average of 19.1x, the lowest since November 2023 [15].

For this group, the best sourced multiple is Damodaran's January 2026 data for US Hotel/Gaming: 14.93x EV/EBITDA for the 63 firms with positive EBITDA and 17.70x for all firms, with 25.71x EV/EBIT on the positive-EBITDA set [11]. That group includes hotels, so it is a rough guide, and it is January data rather than current.

On individual stocks, TIKR puts DraftKings at about 21x forward earnings at the 2 November close, roughly 22x after the rally, near its one-year average [17]. That was before the 21% fall reported after its results, which we did not confirm in a primary source, so the multiple is probably lower now.

Dividends and buybacks are part of the value case at the mature operators: Las Vegas Sands raised its 2027 dividend 20% to $1.44 per share a year [1], Wynn pays $0.25 a quarter [6] and Aristocrat's full-year dividend was 101 cents, up 8.6% [8]. Debt levels (Flutter 4.6x [4], Light & Wonder 3.3x [7]) mean equity is sensitive to small changes in profit.

Price action has been poor for the online names. DraftKings was down about 33% this year as of early November, mostly on fears that prediction markets will take bettors, then rose 14% in a week after Flutter's comments [17]. Brokerage downgrades and a sharp post-earnings fall followed, which we saw only in secondary coverage.

Flutter reported revenue that missed estimates, cut guidance and paused buybacks [17][4]. I did not find sourced year-to-date share performance for Flutter, Las Vegas Sands, MGM or Wynn, so I do not claim relative strength for the resort names.

Buybacks show where management sees value. Las Vegas Sands repurchased about 21M shares at a weighted average of $45.31 for $950M [1], MGM's share count fell to 251.6M from 258.3M at year-end [3], Wynn bought back 627,475 shares at $92.61 [6], and Light & Wonder bought none in the quarter [7]. Flutter paused its program for the foreseeable future [4].

I could not open a current ETF source with flows or assets for gaming funds, and found no sourced short-interest figures, so there is no verified read on flows or positioning. Our judgment is that sentiment is cautious on online betting because of prediction markets and cautious on Macao because of five months of declines [9][17].
